Jensen Huang joked on stage that the CEO of a $3.25 billion AI company will always be his intern, and there's a footnote in a 2023 Nvidia research paper that says he's right.

The CEO is Robin Rombach, who runs Black Forest Labs. Page one of that paper says Robin and two of his future cofounders, Andreas Blattmann and Tim Dockhorn, did the work during internships at NVIDIA.

And the intern project was about cars. They trained on 683,060 real driving clips from Nvidia's own dataset, with the goal of building a simulator that could spit out endless fake road footage for self-driving systems to practice on.

Their trick was cheap and pretty clever. Training a video model from scratch costs a fortune, so they took an image model that already knew what a car looks like, froze it, and slipped in thin new layers whose only job was learning how one frame flows into the next. The same move turned Stable Diffusion, which Robin co-invented, into a text-to-video model.

That idea followed them out the door. Andreas was first author on Stable Video Diffusion at Stability AI, and in 2024 all three left to start BFL.

In July they shipped FLUX 3, one model trained on images, video, audio and robot actions. Its video backbone now runs robots doing car door assembly at Audi, on a single Nvidia RTX 5090, in under 80 milliseconds. So a side project about fake car footage grew into a model that helps put real cars together.

Jensen's got another reason to love this guy. Robin's whole career has been about making image AI cheaper. His PhD breakthrough, latent diffusion, squeezes a 512x512 image from 786,432 numbers down to 16,384 before the model does any real work. That's 48x less to crunch, and it's a big reason image generation left the data center and started running on gaming PCs.

Cheaper image AI pulled in way more users and way more GPU hours. Grok's first image generator ran on FLUX, and Meta, Adobe, Canva and Microsoft all build on it too. Nvidia sells the chips underneath every bit of that, and it invested in BFL's Series A on top of it.

Three interns wrote one paper about fake driving videos, and three years later they're running a $3.25 billion lab that Nvidia owns a piece of, with its newest model driving robots on an Nvidia card. Jensen was playing the line for laughs, and he wasn't exaggerating one bit.

1/  This one is somewhat older paper (DL lifecycle wise) but I think this is an important regularization idea to combat reward hacking! I’ve personally done this (before even reading this paper) and it’s stabilizes the loss landscape. 

DDRL: keep training on data while doing RL. They combine reward maximization with the usual diffusion loss on real/synthetic samples. That denoising loss helps keep generations realistic as the model learns to get higher rewards.
